newsitem.title: Albania: Protesters confront police in southern Albania.
newsitem.headline: Protesters confront police in southern Albania.

text.p: Thousands of Albanian investors duped by pyramid investment schemes staged fresh protests in this southern port city on Wednesday to demand refunds and the resignation of the right-wing government.

Police used water cannon and fired into the air to break up about 3,000 marchers in the first clash since widespread rioting less than two weeks ago in Europe's poorest country. Police bundled about 10 people into vans.
At least three people suffered minor injuries.

The protesters, who denounced right-wing President Sali Berisha, threw stones at police and managed to regroup in a central square. Riot police initially stood opposite them but later withdrew to nearby trucks.
"Berisha is a thief. We'll hang you!" shouted the protesters, many of whom had poured life savings into the schemes. "Resign, resign!" chanted others.
Hospital officials said three demonstrators were treated for minor injuries. State radio said some protesters had been armed and one policeman had been shot and injured.
Reuter correspondent Marko Bello saw no protesters with weapons, but observed bullet holes in a curbside kiosk and two spent cartridges next to it.
"The government has just kept on lying to us," said Besim Aliaj, who said he had tied up the equivalent of $170,000. Like many protesters, he had earned his money in Italy.
Police set up roadblocks on approaches to Vlore and refused to let through cars with out-of-town registrations. Tirana and other cities were quiet, though police were out in force.
The protest was sparked by the collapse on Tuesday of the Gjallica investment scheme, hugely popular in southern Albania.
Newspapers reported that between $350 million to $500 million was tied up in the Gjallica fund. Locals believe as much as $2 billion is believed to be invested in all the various pyramids.
Investors have begun receiving refunds of 50 to 60 percent of their investments in two of the collapsed schemes.
But the procedure was chaotic. Many people were turned away because they did not have the correct documents or refused to settle for only a portion of their lost money.
Berisha has pledged to help the worst-hit investors, like those who sold homes to pump money into the schemes.
He told the Paris daily Le Figaro the collapses were "a perverse effect" of post-communist freedom.
"We are going to open an investigation," he said. "I cannot say (the money) is in Albania."

Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi told state television his government would help investors but rejected a petition by 900,000 Gjallica investors demanding that the country's leaders sell off a power station to pay them back.
"This is completely absurd," he said. "People accepted the profits, they should now accept losses with patience."
Many Vlore demonstrators said they would remain in the square at least overnight to press for their cash. Some vowed to march on Tirana if they received no reply within five days.
Demonstrators set fire last month to government buildings around the country. About 150 people were arrested and prosecutors have threatened long prison terms.

In the six years since the fall of eastern Europe's most repressive communist regime, virtually every family in the country of 3.4 million poured money into pyramid schemes which promised, and paid for a time, high regular interest.

Berisha's Democratic Party retained power last May in elections denounced by observers as fraudulent. He rejects charges that his government failed to warn investors about the pitfalls of pyramid programmes.
